on pages 2 and 3.
How printed books began
The revolutionary invention of movable type
In Europe before the beginning of the 15th
century there was no way of producing
books except to copy them by hand. This
made them extremely expensive; few
people had ever seen a book, and fewer still
could read. However, in the great flowering
of European culture in the 15th and 16th
centuries, the period known as the
Renaissance, this changed, as the invention
of movable ‘type’ made it possible to
produce a large number of copies of any
given book much more quickly. These
books cost relatively little to buy and so
could be circulated more widely.
The first European typographer was the
German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg
(c.1400 — 1468) of Mainz in Germany.
Around the middle of the 1400s, he had the
idea of making ‘printing types’, small
square pieces of metal, each of which had
the reverse image of a letter of the alphabet
carved on its surface. Soon, however,
instead of being individually carved, the
‘types’ were cast from molten metal, so that
they did not take so long to produce. A
complete set of types, representing the
alphabet, was called a ‘fount’, and included
a number of pieces of type for each letter.
Naturally, the printer needed more types for
letters like E, which are used frequently,
than he did for infrequent letters like X.
The types were placed in trays in
special chests or cases stacked vertically,
with the capital letters in the case on top
(which is why we still call them uppercase
letters), and the small letters in the lower
cases. The types were taken out of their
cases one by one and used to compose
words and sentences, held tightly in place
inside a square frame. This frame, which
contained a number of pages, was then
loaded into a printing press and coated with
ink. A sheet of paper was pressed firmly
against the metal surface of the rows of
type, and the image made by the ink, which
reversed the images of the letters to make
them readable, was a printed sheet. The
initial copy off the press, called a ‘proof’,
was read for mistakes, and those that were
found were corrected by shifting the types.
After that, the printers could turn out as
many copies of that sheet and the
subsequent sheets as they needed for the
book, and since each of the sheets was
identical to the others, when they were
folded to produce the right sequence of
pages, each page of each of the books that
resulted was also identical to the same page
in all the others. After the printing of each
sheet was finished, the metal types were
taken out of their frame and put back in
their cases ready to be used again.
The earliest printed books are called
incunabula, because printing was in its
infancy in those days, and incunabula is the
Latin word for the cradles in which
newborn babies slept. These books are very
rare and valuable today.
Sometime early in the 1460s,
Gutenberg’s invention crossed the Alps into
Italy, carried by a train of mules and
accompanied by two enterprising German
typographers from Mainz, named
Sweynheym and Pannartz. They did not
immediately make for Rome, but halted
instead at a monastery at Subiaco. There
they found all the right conditions for the
new art: plenty of space, a rich library of

manuscripts waiting to be transformed into
printed books, and learned monks skilled in
the traditional arts of manuscript book
production such as illuminating* and
binding. The two printers laboured
intensively at Subiaco, but later moved on,
turning up a few years later in Rome, at the
house of the Massimo family, who were
merchants and bankers.
The Massimo home was near the book
industry district in Rome, where the
workshops of manuscript copiers and book
dealers were located. These workers
greeted the new art of typography with
enthusiasm, and printed books spread
rapidly as merchants and bankers saw the
potential for profit that they held. In the
space of ten years, around 160,000 books
were printed in Rome. At first,
typographers sought to reproduce the work
of professional copyists as faithfully as
possible, since their books were to be read
by a public that had never known anything
but manuscripts. Customers who had had
access to books before wanted something
that they were familiar with, and refused at
first to do without the rich colours and
elaborate capital letters of the illuminated
manuscript. After printing, therefore, the
production of the text was completed by the
illuminators, who painted individual
coloured pictures and letters in the spaces
that the printers had left empty for that
purpose.
Around 1500, however, in Venice,
Manuzio, a local book dealer, began to use
metal type to produce simpler pages with
elegant sloping type based on the
handwriting of the Italian writer Petrarch.
Manuzio also abandoned the imitation of
costly, large-format manuscripts, producing
instead accessible, small-format books
which were less expensive: books for the
majority of people, even those of moderate
means. Written text which had previously
been the privileged possession of a few thus
became available to a much wider section
of society.
The introduction of printing with
movable type marked a shift similar to the
one brought about in our lifetime by the
introduction of the computer. It not only
changed the book, but also enabled great
social change.
* illuminating: the illustration and decoration of manuscripts
